newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HEALTH A MAJOR FOCUS IN BUDGET

Big health care cuts are expected to be a major part of tomorrow night's Federal Budget. Cuts to pharmaceutical benefits are expected to pour hundreds of millions of dollars into Treasury coffers, while childcare benefit also looks set for cuts. Patients will have to pay more for expensive brands of drugs, the Government hoping this will encourage the use of cheaper generic drugs, and force drug companies to lower prices. In other health changes, patients will be able to lodge Medicare claims from doctors' surgeries, even if the doctor doesn't bulk bill. And funds will be allocated for public health, research, and hepatitis B vaccinations for children.
BENEFIT CUTS AND SAVINGS INITIATIVE IN BUDGET

Tomorrow's Federal Budget is expected to include initiatives to boost savings, funded by money set aside by the former Labor Government for tax cuts. Treasurer Peter Costello says his second budget will consolidate the work of his first, although this year's cuts won't be as deep.

Childcare and pharmaceutical benefits are expected to face cuts worth hundreds of millions of dollars, with health cuts to total A$1-1/2 billion over four years. However, there will be some new funding for health, allowing patients to lodge Medicare claims at doctors' surgeries, and to pay for hepatitis B vaccinations.
Mr Costello is also optimistic about economic growth and unemployment for the coming year.
GRAZIER SAYS PM NEEDS TO SEE OPPOSITION

United Graziers President, Larry Acton, says it's important for the Prime Minister to be shown the extent of opposition, when he attends a meeting in Longreach on Saturday to sell his ten point plan on Native Title. It'll be the first direct sell of the plan by Mr Howard and his deputy, Tim Fischer.
Mr Acton is calling on those who have shown their support so far to himself and the Queensland Premier, to attend the meeting.
CLEAN-UP AFTER SYDNEY STORMS

The clean-up is continuing after yesterday's gale force winds which lashed metropolitan Sydney and much of the state's coastline. Gale force winds and rough seas kept emergency services busy, with the fire brigade attending around 500 emergencies during the day and the State Emergency Service 1,000.
TWO PRIESTS ATTACKED IN SYDNEY OVERNIGHT

There's been an attack on two priests north-west of Sydney overnight. A 67-year old priest and his 36-year old assistant were taking the day's collection money from St James Church, Muswellbrook, to the nearby presbytery early last night. Police say two men with balaclavas approached the priests, hitting them with baseball bats.

The thieves ran off with the collection bags, leaving the older priest with a severed ear and the younger priest with a broken arm. They were taken to Muswellbrook Hospital and are now in a stable condition.
Police investigating shooting deaths in Victoria

In north-west Victoria, Homocide Squad detectives have arrived in Bereford, about 15 kms north of Swan Hill, to investigate the shooting deaths of three men at two properties overnight. About four o'clock this morning, they found the bodies of two men and about half an hour later, found the body of the third man at a property a short distance away.
Their identities have yet to be established, and Police are calling on the public for information on a cream Holden Camira, with the registration ECB 632.
NAB SURVEY SEES BUSINESS CONDITIONS DETERIORATE

The National Bank's latest business survey says business conditions and confidence deteriorated slightly in April. The monthly survey says the pickup in Australian business activity is yet to eventuate, with annual growth around two-and-a-half to three-percent.
The Bank says while the services sector continues to perform relatively well, manufacturing, retailing and wholesaling continue to report poor conditions.
It says business confidence fell from a level of 14-points in the March quarter to 12-point-four points in April.
